([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]), so
$T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$;
in particular all $T_{i,c,t}$ commute with the $K_h$ and with one another
(Verification, step 2.1).

The **Lusztig divided-power integral form** is the $A$-subalgebra

$$U_A:=\bigl\langle E_i^{(r)},\ F_i^{(r)},\ K_h^{\pm1},\ T_{i,c,t}\ \colon\ i\in I,\ r,t\ge0,\ c\in\mathbb Z,\ h\in P^{\vee}\bigr\rangle\ \subseteq\ U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

where $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ are the divided powers of
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $U_A^\pm$
for the $A$-subalgebras generated by the $E_i^{(r)}$ and by the $F_i^{(r)}$,
and $U_A^0$ for the one generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $T_{i,c,t}$.

Then:

(i) $U_A$ contains $E_i=E_i^{(1)}$, $F_i=F_i^{(1)}$ and all $K_h$;

(ii) $U_A$ is a root-graded $A$-subalgebra of the root-graded
$\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]):
with $U_A[\beta]:=U_A\cap U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ one has
$U_A=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_A[\beta]$, each $U_A[\beta]$ is an $A$-submodule,
and $U_A^\pm,U_A^0$ are graded in the same way;

(iii) $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)\cong U_q(\mathfrak g)$ canonically, i.e. the
$\mathbb Q(q)$-span of $U_A$ is all of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$.

The shifted binomials $T_{i,c,t}$ with $c\ne0$ are included because the
divided-power reordering identity of
[[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]] has
coefficients $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$ with a nonconstant index; the specializations at
$q=1$ of these elements are computed in
[[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]],
and the integral triangular decomposition and the specialization are treated
only after this definition.

No freeness of $U_A$ or of its parts over $A$, no independence of the listed
generators, and no triangularity of the products of the three parts is asserted
here. In particular $A$ is not a principal ideal domain (Verification, step
7.1), so no torsion-free-to-free inference over $A$ is permitted anywhere on
this page.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, let
$U_A$ be the integral form with toral part $U_A^0$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]) and let $k$ be a
characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$.
Write $H_i:=T_{i,0,1}$ and $\bar x$ for the image of $x$ in a specialization.

(a) **Algebra level.** The positive toral quotient
$U_A^0\otimes_Ak/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is the polynomial algebra
$k[H_i:i\in I]$, and in it $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$ for all
$c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$
([[lem-rational-local-quantum-halves-and-torus-specialize-at-q-one]](c)).
No residual $K_h$-ambiguity remains after this quotient — the ideal
$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is exactly the kernel of the comparison with
$k[H_i]$ — but it is *not* claimed that $K_h=1$ in the unquotiented
specialization $U_A^0\otimes_Ak$.

(b) **Label-graded lattices.** Let $M$ be a $P$-graded type-one
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module with label grading $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let
$M_A=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}(M_A\cap M_\mu)$ be a $U_A$-stable $A$-submodule that
is graded in the *lattice's own* sense, i.e. it is the direct sum of its
intersections with the label spaces. Then, on $M_A\otimes_Ak$, the operators
induced by $E_i,F_i$ (and all of $U_A$) satisfy: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$ for
every $h\in P^{\vee}$; $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ acts on the image of $M_A\cap M_\mu$ by
the integer $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$; and
$[\bar E_i,\bar F_j]=\delta_{ij}\bar H_i$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar E_j]=a_{ij}\bar E_j$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar F_j]=-a_{ij}\bar F_j$, where $\bar H_i$ acts on the image of
$M_A\cap M_\mu$ by the integer $\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$.

The grading hypothesis in (b) is a real hypothesis on the lattice: it is not
inferred from the mere fact that $M_A$ spans a weight module. All divisions
that occur are performed inside the DVR
$R=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}$ (units $[r]_i!$ and $q_i^{\pm1}$); no vanishing
denominator $q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is substituted by $q=1$.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

derivations.claim: Divided powers multiply. By definition $E^{(2)}E^{(1)}=\frac{E^{2}}{[2]!}\cdot E=\frac{E^{3}}{[2]!}=\frac{[3]!}{[2]!}E^{(3)}=[3]E^{(3)}$ and $F^{(2)}F^{(2)}=\frac{F^{4}}{([2]!)^{2}}=\frac{[4]!}{([2]!)^{2}}F^{(4)}=\binom{4}{2}_iF^{(4)}$, using $[a]!\ne0$ and $x^{(a)}=x^{a}/[a]!$ from [F1]; the general identity $x^{(a)}x^{(b)}=\binom{a+b}{a}_ix^{(a+b)}$ is the same computation.

The commutator and the first binomial. By [F2] and [F3], $EF-FE=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}$, which is exactly $T_{i,0,1}$ by the definition of the toral binomial; more generally the displayed formula for $EF^{(b)}$ is [F2], and at $b=2$ the toral factor is $\frac{(K-K^{-1})+(q^{-2}K-q^{2}K^{-1})}{q^{2}-q^{-2}}$, which equals $T_{i,-1,1}=(Kq^{-1}-K^{-1}q)/(q-q^{-1})$: use $1+q^{-2}=q^{-1}[2]$ and $1+q^2=q[2]$ with $q^2-q^{-2}=[2](q-q^{-1})$. It is an integral toral binomial.

Reordering at $a=b=2$. Setting $a=b=2$ in the general identity of [F3] gives $E^{(2)}F^{(2)}=\sum_{t=0}^{2}F^{(2-t)}T_{i,2t-4,t}E^{(2-t)}=F^{(2)}E^{(2)}+F^{(1)}T_{i,-2,1}E^{(1)}+T_{i,0,2}$ with $T_{i,-2,1}=\frac{Kq^{-2}-K^{-1}q^{2}}{q-q^{-1}}$ and $T_{i,0,2}=\frac{(K-K^{-1})(Kq^{-1}-K^{-1}q)}{(q-q^{-1})(q^{2}-q^{-2})}$ by the product definition. The nontrivial toral factors $T_{i,-2,1}$ and $T_{i,0,2}$ are generators of the integral form, hence lie in $U_A$.

Values on weights and integrality. On a weight vector of weight $\mu$, $T_{i,0,1}$ acts by $[\mu(h_i)]_i$, $T_{i,-2,1}$ by $[\mu(h_i)-2]_i$ and $T_{i,0,2}$ by $\binom{\mu(h_i)}{2}_i$ by [F4]; at $q=1$ these are the integers $\mu(h_i)$, $\mu(h_i)-2$ and $\binom{\mu(h_i)}{2}$. The numerical value $\binom{4}{2}_i=q^{-4}+q^{-2}+2+q^{2}+q^{4}$ is nonzero in $A$ by [F5], so the product formula of step 1.1 exhibits a nonzero integral coefficient, and no division by a vanishing denominator occurs: every expression used is an element of $U_A$ or a polynomial identity valid in $\mathbb Q(q)$. No choice is used; the computation is a finite expansion in $A_i$, with the $a=b=2$ identity justified by the locally proved reordering supplier.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1 computes the products of degree two and four; the empty product case a=b=0 is the general identity x^{(0)}x^{(0)}=1 read off from [F1], where the binomial coefficient is 1.

step 1.1 uses [a]!=0 so no division by zero occurs, and step 2.1 evaluates the toral scalars at q=1 as integers; the element T_{i,-2,1} of step 1.3 is nonzero on a generic weight because its numerator Kq^{-2}-K^{-1}q^2 does not vanish identically.
the case a=b=1 appears in step 1.2: EF-FE=T_{i,0,1}, and step 2.1 evaluates the associated scalars [mu(h_i)], mu(h_i)-2, binom(mu(h_i),2) as their q=1 integers.

step 1.3 checks the reordering identity at the specific indices a=b=2 where all three toral factors occur, including the middle factor T_{i,-2,1}, so the degenerate term is verified rather than skipped.
step 1.3 expands the sum t=0,1,2 at both ends F^{(2)}E^{(2)} and T_{i,0,2}, and step 2.1 checks the values of the endpoint scalars at q=1.

boundaries.reason: every computation is an explicit product or specialization in the rank-one algebra; no family is selected and no choice principle is used.
the example verifies identities and computes specializations; it states no biconditional, its assertions being the two products, the reordering identity and the integrality table.
no converse is claimed; the q=1 integrality values of step 2.1 are numerical evaluations of the same operators, not the reverse direction of an implication.

Empty divided powers and negative integer weight values respect those conventions. This is finite rank-one algebra with no AC; Stanford pp.9–10 matches the product and equal-exponent reordering background.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum with $a_{ii}=2$ for
all $i$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with Borel subalgebra
$U_q^{\ge0}=U_q^0U_q^+$ and negative half $U_q^-$
([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]). Fix
$\lambda\in P$ and let $\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)$ be the
**Borel character module** on which $K_h$ acts by the scalar
$q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}$ and every $E_i$ acts as $0$ (the character is a
well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra homomorphism
$\chi_\lambda\colon U_q^{\ge0}\to\mathbb Q(q)$, Verification, step 1.1). The
**quantum Verma module** is the induced module

$$M(\lambda):=U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U_q^{\ge0}}\mathbb Q(q)_\lambda,$$

a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module, with distinguished vector
$v_\lambda:=1\otimes1$ ([[def-quotient-ring]] for the quotient/induction
conventions).

Then (Verification, steps 2.1 and 3.1):

(i) $M(\lambda)$ carries the **canonical $P$-label grading**
$M(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M(\lambda)_\mu$ with
$M(\lambda)_{\lambda-\nu}=U_q^-[-\nu]v_\lambda$ for $\nu\in Q_+$ and
$M(\lambda)_\mu=0$ otherwise; each $M(\lambda)_\mu$ is finite dimensional
(there are only finitely many words in the $F_i$ of a given root degree), and
$M(\lambda)_\lambda=\mathbb Q(q)v_\lambda$ is the highest line. With this
grading $M(\lambda)$ is a $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and $v_\lambda$ is a highest
weight vector: $K_hv_\lambda=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v_\lambda$,
$E_iv_\lambda=0$, $M(\lambda)=U_q(\mathfrak g)v_\lambda$.

(ii) (Universal property) For every left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $V$ and every
$v\in V$ with $K_hv=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}v$ and $E_iv=0$ for all $h,i$
there is a unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $M(\lambda)\to V$ with
$v_\lambda\mapsto v$; if $V=U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is cyclic, this map is
surjective. When $V$ is a $P$-graded type-one module and $v\in V_\lambda$, the
map is grading-preserving.

(iii) The sum $N(\lambda)$ of all proper graded submodules of $M(\lambda)$ is a
proper graded submodule, and

$$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/N(\lambda)$$

is the **simple highest weight quotient**: it has no nonzero proper graded
submodule, and it is the unique simple graded quotient of $M(\lambda)$ up to
isomorphism ([[def-submodule]]). Thus the maximal proper submodule occurring
here is the sum of *all* proper graded submodules, not an arbitrarily chosen
maximal one; no choice is used.

If the pairing separates $P$, then every submodule of $M(\lambda)$ is graded,
$N(\lambda)$ is the unique maximal proper submodule, and $L(\lambda)$ is the
ordinary simple (not only graded-simple) quotient: this is the usual simple
weight-module quotient of the Verma module over a separating torus
(Verification, step 4.1).

The contravariant Cartan-projection lemma
`lem-cartan-projection-constructs-the-quantum-verma-contravariant-form`
identifies $N(\lambda)$ with the radical of the normalized Verma contravariant
form and gives the canonical normalized form on $L(\lambda)$; for $\lambda$
dominant integral, the existence theorem
`thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique` proves the
ordinary simplicity and the universal integrable conclusions. Both are
declared obligations of those later items, not assumptions here.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, step 2.2).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$, an index $i\in I$, and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. Let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra and let $A_i$ be the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$ ([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]); write $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$ for the divided powers of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]].

(i) The assignment $e\mapsto E_i$, $f\mapsto F_i$, $k\mapsto K_i$, $k^{-1}\mapsto K_i^{-1}$ defines an algebra isomorphism from the standard rank-one algebra $\mathbb A$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, presented by $e,f,k^{\pm1}$ with $kek^{-1}=q_i^2e$, $kfk^{-1}=q_i^{-2}f$ and $[e,f]=(k-k^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ onto $A_i$; the images of the monomials $F_i^aK_i^mE_i^b$ ($a,b\ge0$, $m\in\mathbb Z$) are linearly independent in $U_q(\mathfrak g)$, being images of the PBW monomials of the triangular decomposition ([[thm-triangular-decomposition-of-a-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]).

$$E_iF_i^{(b)}=F_i^{(b)}E_i+\frac{F_i^{(b-1)}}{q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}\bigl(q_i^{-2s}K_i-q_i^{2s}K_i^{-1}\bigr);$$
iterating it computes $E_i^{(a)}F_i^{(b)}$ as a finite sum of monomials $F_i^{(b-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{(a-t)}$ ($0\le t\le\min(a,b)$) with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support contained in
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a

$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is

the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

derivations.claim: Basis and action. By [F1], the ordinary-power vectors $u_t=F^tu_0$ are a basis, with $Ku_t=q^{m-2t}u_t$ and $Fu_t=u_{t+1}$. Evaluating [F2] on $u_0$ gives $Eu_t=\bigl(\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}(q^{m-2s}-q^{-m+2s})/(q-q^{-1})\bigr)u_{t-1}$. The geometric sums satisfy $\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}q^{-2s}=q^{-(t-1)}[t]$ and $\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}q^{2s}=q^{t-1}[t]$, so $Eu_t=[t][m-t+1]u_{t-1}$. Dividing by $[t]!$ gives the displayed actions on $v_t=F^{(t)}u_0$.

The dominant quotient. For $m\ge0$, $Eu_{m+1}=0$ by step 1.1. The tail spanned by $u_t$, $t\ge m+1$, is stable under $E,F,K^{\pm1}$ by those formulas, and it is exactly the submodule generated by $u_{m+1}$ because repeated $F$ generates every tail vector. Therefore its quotient has basis $v_0,\ldots,v_m$ and the stated truncated divided-power actions. For a nonzero vector $x=\sum_{t=0}^T c_tv_t$ with largest occupied index $T\le m$, $E^Tx=c_T\prod_{j=1}^T[m-j+1]v_0\ne0$: lower-index terms are killed. Any submodule containing $x$ contains $v_0$ and then every $v_t$, so the quotient is simple. The empty product covers $T=0$ and $m=0$ gives the trivial module.

The boundary $m=-1$. Here $Ev_t=-[t]v_{t-1}$ for $t\ge1$. For a nonzero finite sum $x=\sum_{t=0}^T c_tv_t$ with $c_T
e0$, $E^Tx=c_T\prod_{j=1}^T(-[j])v_0
e0$, including the empty product when $T=0$. A submodule containing $x$ therefore contains $v_0$ and every $v_t$; $M(-1)$ is simple. It is infinite-dimensional by its basis, and $F^tu_0=u_t
e0$ for all $t$, so it is not integrable. The label $-1$ is integral and is not dominant.

For $m<0$, all scalars $[m-j+1]$, $j\ge1$, are nonzero. The same largest-index argument gives $E^Tx=c_T\prod_{j=1}^T[m-j+1]v_0\ne0$ for each nonzero finite sum. Thus $M(m)=L(m)$ is simple, infinite-dimensional and non-integrable, with integral non-dominant highest weight. The explicit dominant strings in step 2.1 and these negative cases prove all stated conclusions.

boundaries.evidence: the basis of step 1.1 starts at v_0=F^0v_0, the empty power, and the string formula there is the base of the induction for Ev_t.
step 2.2 shows Ev_t=[-t]v_{t-1} is nonzero for t>=1 when m=-1, since [t]!=0; the case m=0 gives the one-dimensional trivial module L(0) of step 2.1.
step 2.1 treats m=1 as the two-dimensional quotient with F^2v_0=0, and step 1.1's string computation is exercised at t=1 to obtain Ev_1=[m]v_0.
Step 2.2 treats m=-1, and step 3.1 treats all m<0, using the largest occupied divided-power index and nonzero raising coefficients.
step 2.1 uses the endpoint t=m+1 where F^{m+1}v_0 becomes a highest vector; step 1.1 sets the other endpoint Ev_0=0.

boundaries.reason: the submodule structure is decided by the vanishing of the explicit scalars [m-t+1]; no selection from nonempty sets or maximality argument occurs.
the example classifies the cases m>=0, m=-1 and m<0 separately; no claim is formulated as a biconditional requiring direction-by-direction proof.
there is no converse to check: irreducibility in steps 2.2 and 3.1 and finite-dimensionality in step 2.1 are direct conclusions rather than two halves of an equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Accepted the reader's explicit standard rank-one datum, distinction between ordinary and divided bases, largest-index raising argument and integral/nondominant wording. Read Example/Facts/Verification 1.1–3.1 and all six cited interfaces. The ordinary basis has E coefficient [t][m-t+1], whereas divided basis has [m-t+1]; K weights are m-2t in both. For m>=0 the singular tail beginning at m+1 is stable and exactly generated by F^(m+1)v; the quotient has m+1 basis vectors. Raising a finite sum from its largest occupied index produces a nonzero top vector, proving ordinary simplicity. For every m<0 the same coefficients never vanish, including m=-1 where they are -[t]; F remains nonnilpotent, proving infinite dimension and nonintegrability. m=0 is trivial, and T=0 uses the empty raising product. Dominance, not integrality, is the essential failed hypothesis. No AC enters this finite-word argument.

citations.quote:
Use the standard rank-one datum $P=\mathbb Z\omega$, $P^\vee=\mathbb Zh$, $\alpha=2\omega$, $\langle\omega,h\rangle=1$ and $d_1=1$. Thus $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ is generated by $E,F,K^{\pm1}$ with $q_1=q$. For $m\in\mathbb Z$, put $\lambda=m\omega$ and write $[t]=(q^t-q^{-t})/(q-q^{-1})$.

The Verma module $M(m)$ has ordinary-power basis $u_t=F^tu_0$, $t\ge0$, where $u_0=v_\lambda$. Its actions are
$$Ku_t=q^{m-2t}u_t,\qquad Fu_t=u_{t+1},\qquad Eu_t=[t][m-t+1]u_{t-1}\quad(t\ge1),\qquad Eu_0=0.$$
The divided-power basis $v_t=F^{(t)}u_0=u_t/[t]!$ instead satisfies
$$Kv_t=q^{m-2t}v_t,\qquad Fv_t=[t+1]v_{t+1},\qquad Ev_t=[m-t+1]v_{t-1}\quad(t\ge1),\qquad Ev_0=0.$$

(a) For $m\ge0$, the submodule generated by $F^{m+1}u_0$ is the tail spanned by $u_t$, $t\ge m+1$. Its quotient $L(m)$ is simple of dimension $m+1$, with divided-power basis $v_0,\ldots,v_m$ and the second set of actions, with $v_{-1}=v_{m+1}=0$. For $m=0$ it is trivial.

(b) For $m=-1$, the raising coefficients in the divided-power basis are $[-t]=-[t]\ne0$ for every $t\ge1$. Hence $M(-1)=L(-1)$ is irreducible, infinite-dimensional and not integrable. Its highest weight is integral and is not dominant.

(c) For every $m<0$, $m-t+1\ne0$ at all $t\ge1$, so the same conclusions hold. Thus dominance in [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]] is essential.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and put $q_i=q^{d_i}$. For $m\in\mathbb N$, define the **$q_i$-integer**

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

and the **$q_i$-factorial**

$$[m]_i!:=\prod_{k=1}^m[k]_i,\qquad [0]_i!:=1.$$

For $0\le r\le m$, define the **Gaussian binomial** $\binom{m}{r}_i:=[m]_i!/([r]_i![m-r]_i!)$, and set it to $0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$. In the published one-parameter convention, write $\binom{m}{r}_t:=\binom{m}{r,m-r}_t$ for the two-part $q$-multinomial coefficient of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]].

For an element $x$ of a unital $\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra and $m\ge0$, define its **divided power at $q_i$** by $x^{(m)}:=x^m/[m]_i!$, so $x^{(0)}=1$ and $x^{(1)}=x$.

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Fix a symmetrizable Cartan datum and $i\in I$, and use the conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $C_{m,r}:=\binom{m}{r}_i$, with $C_{m,r}=0$ when $r<0$ or $r>m$.

(i) **Pascal recurrences.** For $m\ge1$ and every integer $r$,

$$C_{m,r}=q_i^{-r}C_{m-1,r}+q_i^{m-r}C_{m-1,r-1}=q_i^rC_{m-1,r}+q_i^{r-m}C_{m-1,r-1}.$$

(ii) **Symmetry.** For $0\le r\le m$, $C_{m,r}=C_{m,m-r}$.

(iii) **Gauss product formula.** For every $N\ge0$, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q(q)[z]$,

$$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}(1+q_i^{2j}z)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}q_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}z^r.$$

Consequently, for $N\ge1$,

$$\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-1)^rq_i^{r(N-1)}C_{N,r}=0.$$

(iv) **Integrality.** For $0\le r\le m$,

$$C_{m,r}\in q_i^{-r(m-r)}\mathbb Z[q_i^2]\subseteq\mathbb Z[q_i^{\pm1}].$$

Thus every Gaussian quotient is a Laurent polynomial in $q_i$ with integer coefficients, and the Pascal recurrences hold in that Laurent polynomial ring.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum
group with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]) with $q_i=q^{d_i}$ and
$K_i=K_{d_ih_i}$, and set

$$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\ \subseteq\ \mathbb Q(q),$$

the image of the Laurent polynomial ring $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t]_{S}$ of
[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]] under the unital ring homomorphism sending
$t$ to the indeterminate $q$; this homomorphism is injective and $A$ is a
subring of $\mathbb Q(q)$ (Verification, step 1.1). We work over this
commutative domain $A$ inside the field $\mathbb Q(q)$.

For $i\in I$, $c\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\ge0$ define the **toral quantum binomial**

$$T_{i,c,t}:=\begin{bmatrix}K_i;c\\ t\end{bmatrix}:=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\frac{K_iq_i^{\,c-s+1}-K_i^{-1}q_i^{\,-c+s-1}}{q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}}\in U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

the empty product being $T_{i,c,0}:=1$. Each factor is defined in
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ because $q_i^{\,s}-q_i^{\,-s}\ne0$ for $s\ge1$
([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]), so
$T_{i,c,t}$ is a polynomial in $K_i^{\pm1}$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Q(q)$;
in particular all $T_{i,c,t}$ commute with the $K_h$ and with one another
(Verification, step 2.1).

The **Lusztig divided-power integral form** is the $A$-subalgebra

$$U_A:=\bigl\langle E_i^{(r)},\ F_i^{(r)},\ K_h^{\pm1},\ T_{i,c,t}\ \colon\ i\in I,\ r,t\ge0,\ c\in\mathbb Z,\ h\in P^{\vee}\bigr\rangle\ \subseteq\ U_q(\mathfrak g),$$

where $x^{(r)}=x^r/[r]_i!$ are the divided powers of
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]. Write $U_A^\pm$
for the $A$-subalgebras generated by the $E_i^{(r)}$ and by the $F_i^{(r)}$,
and $U_A^0$ for the one generated by the $K_h^{\pm1}$ and the $T_{i,c,t}$.

Then:

(i) $U_A$ contains $E_i=E_i^{(1)}$, $F_i=F_i^{(1)}$ and all $K_h$;

(ii) $U_A$ is a root-graded $A$-subalgebra of the root-graded
$\mathbb Q(q)$-algebra $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ ([[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]):
with $U_A[\beta]:=U_A\cap U_q(\mathfrak g)[\beta]$ one has
$U_A=\bigoplus_{\beta\in Q}U_A[\beta]$, each $U_A[\beta]$ is an $A$-submodule,
and $U_A^\pm,U_A^0$ are graded in the same way;

(iii) $U_A\otimes_A\mathbb Q(q)\cong U_q(\mathfrak g)$ canonically, i.e. the
$\mathbb Q(q)$-span of $U_A$ is all of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$.

The shifted binomials $T_{i,c,t}$ with $c\ne0$ are included because the
divided-power reordering identity of
[[lem-divided-power-and-toral-quantum-binomial-reordering-identities]] has
coefficients $T_{i,2t-a-b,t}$ with a nonconstant index; the specializations at
$q=1$ of these elements are computed in
[[lem-q-one-toral-specialization-identifies-the-classical-cartan-generators]],
and the integral triangular decomposition and the specialization are treated
only after this definition.

No freeness of $U_A$ or of its parts over $A$, no independence of the listed
generators, and no triangularity of the products of the three parts is asserted
here. In particular $A$ is not a principal ideal domain (Verification, step
7.1), so no torsion-free-to-free inference over $A$ is permitted anywhere on
this page.

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, let
$U_A$ be the integral form with toral part $U_A^0$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]) and let $k$ be a
characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$.
Write $H_i:=T_{i,0,1}$ and $\bar x$ for the image of $x$ in a specialization.

(a) **Algebra level.** The positive toral quotient
$U_A^0\otimes_Ak/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is the polynomial algebra
$k[H_i:i\in I]$, and in it $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$ for all
$c\in\mathbb Z$, $t\ge0$
([[lem-rational-local-quantum-halves-and-torus-specialize-at-q-one]](c)).
No residual $K_h$-ambiguity remains after this quotient — the ideal
$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is exactly the kernel of the comparison with
$k[H_i]$ — but it is *not* claimed that $K_h=1$ in the unquotiented
specialization $U_A^0\otimes_Ak$.

(b) **Label-graded lattices.** Let $M$ be a $P$-graded type-one
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module with label grading $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let
$M_A=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}(M_A\cap M_\mu)$ be a $U_A$-stable $A$-submodule that
is graded in the *lattice's own* sense, i.e. it is the direct sum of its
intersections with the label spaces. Then, on $M_A\otimes_Ak$, the operators
induced by $E_i,F_i$ (and all of $U_A$) satisfy: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$ for
every $h\in P^{\vee}$; $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ acts on the image of $M_A\cap M_\mu$ by
the integer $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$; and
$[\bar E_i,\bar F_j]=\delta_{ij}\bar H_i$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar E_j]=a_{ij}\bar E_j$,
$[\bar H_i,\bar F_j]=-a_{ij}\bar F_j$, where $\bar H_i$ acts on the image of
$M_A\cap M_\mu$ by the integer $\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$.

The grading hypothesis in (b) is a real hypothesis on the lattice: it is not
inferred from the mere fact that $M_A$ spans a weight module. All divisions
that occur are performed inside the DVR
$R=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}$ (units $[r]_i!$ and $q_i^{\pm1}$); no vanishing
denominator $q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is substituted by $q=1$.

The grading hypothesis in (b) is a real hypothesis on the lattice: it is not
inferred from the mere fact that $M_A$ spans a weight module. All divisions

$R=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}$ (units $[r]_i!$ and $q_i^{\pm1}$); no vanishing

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a finite symmetrizable Cartan datum, $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$,
$U_A$ the integral form of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], and $k$
a characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$. Let
$\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}}$ be the classical Lie algebra presented by
generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ with the Cartan and Serre relations, its Cartan being
the span of the independent simple coroots
([[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]).

(a) **Halves.** $U_A^\pm\otimes_Ak\cong U(\mathfrak n^\pm)_k$ by
$F_i\mapsto f_i$, respectively $E_i\mapsto e_i$.

(b) **Positive quotient.** The quotient
$(U_A\otimes_Ak)/(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$ is isomorphic to
$U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$; in it $\bar H_i=\bar T_{i,0,1}$ is the
classical coroot generator, $\bar T_{i,c,t}=\binom{H_i+c}{t}$, and the positive
toral quotient is $k[H_i:i\in I]$ with kernel exactly
$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$.

(c) **Operator form.** On every $U_A$-stable label-graded lattice the quotient
action of (b) is automatic: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$, the $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ act by
the integer binomials $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$, and all classical
Cartan and Serre operator relations hold, without any unproved global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness.

(d) **Boundaries.** The unquotiented specialization $U_A\otimes_Ak$ is *not*
identified with $U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$: it retains toral characters,
as the integral $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-representation with $E=F=0$, $K=-1$ shows.
Extra Cartan directions of a regular realization act diagonally on
label-graded modules; they are not fabricated as generators of the toral
integral form, and direct substitution $q=1$ into vanishing denominators
$q_i^s-q_i^{-s}$ is never performed anywhere in this comparison.

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight and let
$\tilde L(\lambda)$ be the nonzero integrable quotient of the Verma module
$M(\lambda)$ of [[lem-quantum-highest-weight-serre-quotient-is-integrable]]
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]]), with
highest vector $v_\lambda$ and label grading
([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]). Put
$R:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q-1)}\subset\mathbb Q(q)$.

(a) **Character.** Every nonzero graded quotient $V$ of $\tilde L(\lambda)$
whose highest line is nonzero is generated by its highest vector and has in
every label the same dimension as the classical simple integrable highest
weight module of the regularized minimal realization of the same Cartan datum
([[lem-finite-support-regularization-of-quantum-label-weight-modules]],
[[thm-kac-moody-verma-module-has-a-unique-simple-quotient]]); in particular the
character is independent of $V$. No global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and
no crystal or global basis is used.

(b) **Uniqueness.** Consequently $\tilde L(\lambda)$ is simple, hence is the
canonical simple highest weight module $L(\lambda)$, and every integrable cyclic
highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ is a quotient of
$L(\lambda)$.

(c) **The $R$-lattice.** For a nonzero highest vector $v$ of $V$, the lattice
$V_R:=\sum_wR\,F_wv$, summed over all ordinary words $w$ in the negative
generators, is stable under every generator of the integral form $U_A$ of
[[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], is finite free over $R$ on each
label weight, and is generated by $v$ under $U_A$ after extension to $R$; its $q=1$ fibre
$V_R/(q-1)V_R$ is the classical simple integrable highest weight module of the
regularized minimal realization. Here the Gaussian binomials
$\binom{m}{r}_i$ of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]
are $R$-valued at integer labels, and the divided-power denominators
$[r]_i!$ and $q_i^{\pm1}$ are $R$-units.

derivations.claim: The lattice. Put $v_t=F^{(t)}v_0$, $0\le t\le m$. These vectors are $\mathbb Q(q)$-independent by [F1], so $V_A=\bigoplus_{t=0}^mAv_t$ is free. For $r\ge0$, repeated application of the string formulas and division by $[r]!$ give $F^{(r)}v_t=\binom{t+r}{r}_qv_{t+r}$ if $t+r\le m$, and $0$ otherwise; likewise $E^{(r)}v_t=\binom{m-t+r}{r}_qv_{t-r}$ if $r\le t$, and $0$ otherwise. The coefficients are Laurent integral by the Gaussian identities. Also $K^{\pm1}v_t=q^{\pm(m-2t)}v_t$, and $T_{c,s}v_t=\binom{m-2t+c}{s}_qv_t\in Av_t$, including negative upper labels by the generalized-binomial identity of [F3]'s supplier. Thus every generator of $U_A$ preserves $V_A$. Each $v_t$ is obtained by a divided power from $v_0$, so $V_A=U_Av_0$.

Specialization. Base change of the explicit free basis to $k$ gives $\bar V=V_A\otimes_Ak$ has the $k$-basis $\bar v_0,\dots,\bar v_m$ and dimension $m+1$. Substituting $q=1$ is legitimate here because the action matrices in the basis $F^{(t)}v_0$ are known explicitly with entries in $A$: $\bar K=\mathrm{id}$, $\bar F\bar v_t=(t+1)\bar v_{t+1}$, $\bar E\bar v_t=(m-t+1)\bar v_{t-1}$ and $\bar T_{c,s}\bar v_t=\binom{m-2t+c}{s}\bar v_t$, in particular $\bar T_{0,1}\bar v_t=(m-2t)\bar v_t$; this is the operator form of [F3] on the graded lattice.

$$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\ \subseteq\ \mathbb Q(q),$$

$$[m]_i:=\frac{q_i^m-q_i^{-m}}{q_i-q_i^{-1}},\qquad [0]_i:=0,$$

The symmetric convention and the published asymmetric convention are related, for $m\ge0$ and $0\le r\le m$, by

$$[m]_i=q_i^{-(m-1)}[m]_{q_i^2},\qquad \binom{m}{r}_i=q_i^{-r(m-r)}\binom{m}{r}_{q_i^2}.$$

In particular $[m]_i$ is invariant under $q_i\mapsto q_i^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the symmetrizer only through $q_i=q^{d_i}$.

Use the standard rank-one datum $P=\mathbb Z\omega$, $P^\vee=\mathbb Zh$, $\alpha=2\omega$, $\langle\omega,h\rangle=1$ and $d_1=1$. Thus $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ is generated by $E,F,K^{\pm1}$ with $q_1=q$. For $m\in\mathbb Z$, put $\lambda=m\omega$ and write $[t]=(q^t-q^{-t})/(q-q^{-1})$.

The divided-power basis $v_t=F^{(t)}u_0=u_t/[t]!$ instead satisfies
$$Kv_t=q^{m-2t}v_t,\qquad Fv_t=[t+1]v_{t+1},\qquad Ev_t=[m-t+1]v_{t-1}\quad(t\ge1),\qquad Ev_0=0.$$

$U_A$ the integral form of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]], and $k$
a characteristic-zero field regarded as an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$. Let
$\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}}$ be the classical Lie algebra presented by
generators $e_i,f_i,h_i$ with the Cartan and Serre relations, its Cartan being
the span of the independent simple coroots
([[thm-serre-presentation-of-a-kac-moody-algebra]]).

(a) **Halves.** $U_A^\pm\otimes_Ak\cong U(\mathfrak n^\pm)_k$ by
$F_i\mapsto f_i$, respectively $E_i\mapsto e_i$.

$(K_h-1:h\in P^{\vee})$.

(c) **Operator form.** On every $U_A$-stable label-graded lattice the quotient
action of (b) is automatic: $\bar K_h=\mathrm{id}$, the $\bar T_{i,c,t}$ act by
the integer binomials $\binom{\langle\mu,h_i\rangle+c}{t}$, and all classical
Cartan and Serre operator relations hold, without any unproved global

identified with $U(\mathfrak g_{\mathrm{der}})_k$: it retains toral characters,

Let $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ be the rank-one Cartan datum with $\lambda(h_1)=m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$,

$Kv_t=q^{m-2t}v_t$, $Fv_t=[t+1]_qv_{t+1}$,
$Ev_t=[m-t+1]_qv_{t-1}$
([[ex-quantum-verma-and-simple-modules-for-sl-two]],
[[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Let
$A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let
$V_A=\sum_{t=0}^mAF^{(t)}v_0\subseteq L(m)$ be the lattice generated by the
highest weight vector under the divided powers of the integral form $U_A$
([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]). Let $k$ be a field of
characteristic $0$, made an $A$-algebra by $q\mapsto1$, and put

$$\bar K=1,\qquad \bar F\bar v_t=(t+1)\bar v_{t+1},\qquad \bar E\bar v_t=(m-t+1)\bar v_{t-1},\qquad \bar T_{0,1}\bar v_t=(m-2t)\bar v_t,$$

By [F2], in the two-dimensional module $L(1)$ the element $K$ acts as $\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})$ and $x=T_{0,1}$ acts as $\operatorname{diag}([1]_q,[-1]_q)=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, a nonzero operator. Substituting $q=1$ into the matrix of $K$ gives the identity operator $\operatorname{diag}(1,1)$, so the operator induced by $x$ is not obtained by substituting $q=1$ into the numerator and denominator of the rational expression: the naive substitution loses the entire Cartan action.

Further witnesses. (i) The Gaussian integers: $[m]_q=\frac{q^m-q^{-m}}{q-q^{-1}}$ has numerator and denominator vanishing at $q=1$ for every $m\ne0$, while the correct specialization is the integer $m$; for example $\binom{2}{1}_q=[2]_q=(q^2-q^{-2})/(q-q^{-1})$ gives $0/0$ by separate substitution, whereas its Laurent expression $q+q^{-1}$ specializes to $2$. (ii) The divided-power commutation coefficient $\frac{1}{q^b-q^{-b}}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q^{-2s}K-q^{2s}K^{-1})$ of [F3]: its numerator and denominator both vanish at $q=1$, yet on a weight vector $w$ of weight $\mu$ with $E_iw=0$ its action is the finite value $[\mu(h_i)-b+1]_q\mapsto\mu(h_i)-b+1$ given by the string formula. Each of these elements lies in $U_A$ and has a well-defined specialized operator through the integral form.

The correct statement. By [F4], specialization is the base change $U_A\otimes_Ak$ with $q\mapsto1$: it is defined on elements of the integral form (and on operator matrices on graded lattices, whose entries are Laurent polynomials), and the cancellations in Steps 1.1-1.3 are performed inside $U_A$ before any reduction. On the label-graded lattice $Av_0\oplus Av_1$ of $L(1)$, the action factors through the positive quotient by $K-1$, and $T_{0,1}$ induces the classical coroot operator $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ by [F4]. The coroot identification is made in that quotient or on these lattice operators; it is not asserted in the full unquotiented algebra. No choice is used; every witness is an explicit finite matrix computation.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In $H_v(n)$ there is a unique $A$-semilinear unital ring involution, denoted by a bar, with $\bar v=v^{-1}$ and $\overline{H_{s_i}}=H_{s_i}^{-1}$. It is multiplicative and satisfies $\overline{\overline{H_w}}=H_w$ and $\overline{H_w}=H_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$ for every $w\in S_n$; consequently each $H_w$ is invertible and $\overline{H_{w^{-1}}}=H_w^{-1}$.

For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

derivations.claim:
**Construct the coefficients.** Fix $w$ and descend on $d=\ell(w)-\ell(x)$ over the finite lower Bruhat ideal $\{x:x\le w\}$, starting with $p_{w,w}=1$. Suppose $x<w$ and $p_{y,w}$ has been constructed for every $x<y\le w$, satisfying $p_{y,w}=\sum_{y\le z\le w}r_{y,z}\overline{p_{z,w}}$. Put $a_x:=\sum_{x<y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{p_{y,w}}$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{a_x}&=\sum_{x<y\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}p_{y,w}=\sum_{x<y\le z\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}r_{y,z}\overline{p_{z,w}}\\&=-\sum_{x<z\le w}r_{x,z}\overline{p_{z,w}}=-a_x.\end{aligned}$$
The second equality uses the induction equations; for $x<z$, the identity $\bar R R=I$ makes the sum over $x\le y\le z$ zero, and its omitted diagonal term is $\overline{r_{x,x}}r_{x,z}=r_{x,z}$. Write $a_x=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\gamma_m v^m$. Anti-invariance gives $\gamma_{-m}=-\gamma_m$ and $\gamma_0=0$. Define $p_{x,w}:=\sum_{m>0}\gamma_m v^m$. Then $p_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ and $p_{x,w}-\overline{p_{x,w}}=a_x$. The induction is finite and uses no choice principle. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

**Bar invariance and the coefficient equations.** Set $\underline H_w:=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$. The coefficient of $H_x$ in $\overline{\underline H_w}$ is $\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{p_{y,w}}$. For $x=w$ this is $1$; for $x<w$ it is $\overline{p_{x,w}}+a_x=p_{x,w}$ by step 1.1. If $x\not\le w$, no $y\le w$ can satisfy $x\le y$, so support from [F3] gives coefficient zero. Thus $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and $p_{x,w}=\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{p_{y,w}}$, which is the bar-duality formula. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

**Uniqueness.** If two bar-invariant elements satisfy the triangular condition, their difference is a bar-fixed sum $h=\sum_{y<w}c_yH_y$ with each $c_y\in v\mathbb Z[v]$. If $h\ne0$, choose a Bruhat-maximal $x$ in its finite support. The coefficient of $H_x$ in $\overline h$ is $\overline{c_x}$: no supported $y>x$ contributes, and support of $r_{x,y}$ requires $x\le y$. Since $h=\overline h$, $c_x=\overline{c_x}$; but $v\mathbb Z[v]$ and $v^{-1}\mathbb Z[v^{-1}]$ intersect only in $0$, a contradiction. Thus the element is unique. The construction also gives $p_{w,w}=1$ and $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

**Basis.** The transition from $(H_w)$ to $(\underline H_w)$ is unitriangular on the finite Bruhat poset: each $\underline H_w=H_w+\sum_{y<w}p_{y,w}H_y$. A finite unitriangular matrix over $A$ is invertible, so $(\underline H_w)_{w\in S_n}$ is an $A$-basis. [F1, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

**Degree, leading term, and parity.** Induct on $d=\ell(w)-\ell(x)$, with $p_{w,w}=1$. For $x<w$, the equation in step 1.1 has $a_x=\sum_{x<y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{p_{y,w}}$. By [F3] and induction, every term has exponents congruent to $d$ modulo $2$. The term $y=w$ is $r_{x,w}$, whose highest term is $v^d$ with coefficient $1$. For each $y<w$, put $d_1=\ell(y)-\ell(x)$ and $d_2=\ell(w)-\ell(y)\ge1$, so $d_1+d_2=d$; the highest degree of $r_{x,y}\overline{p_{y,w}}$ is at most $d_1-1\le d-2$, since $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$. Therefore $a_x$ has highest term $v^d$ with coefficient $1$ and only exponents of parity $d$. As $p_{x,w}$ is its positive-degree part by step 1.1, it follows that $p_{x,w}=v^d+$ terms of strictly smaller degree and $p_{x,w}\in v^d\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$. This proves the degree and parity clauses. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

**Inverse-index symmetry.** By [F4], $\flat(\underline H_w)$ is bar-fixed. By [F5], inversion preserves Bruhat order, so this element has the form $H_{w^{-1}}+\sum_{y<w}p_{y,w}H_{y^{-1}}$ with lower terms in $v\mathbb Z[v]$. Uniqueness from step 3.1 gives $\flat(\underline H_w)=\underline H_{w^{-1}}$. Comparing coefficients yields $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
